extracted.intended_audience: writers, screenwriters, students and readers seeking guidance on narrative/story structure
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on structuring a narrative into three parts (Setup, Confrontation, Resolution), including the functions of acts, the dramatic question, inciting incident, rising action, character arc, climax, and resolution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three-act structure (overall model)
rubrics_metrics.description: The three-act structure is a model used in narrative fiction that divides a story into three parts (acts), often called the Setup, the Confrontation, and the Resolution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Presented as an overarching model for dramatic structure (widely used in screenwriting); attributed to Syd Field. Use this division to plan major story phases and transitions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dramatic question
rubrics_metrics.description: As the story moves along, the plot usually progresses in such a way as to pose a major dramatic question.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'Will the boy get the girl?' 'Will the hero save the day?' 'Will the detective solve the mystery?' 'Will the criminal be caught by law enforcement and brought to justice?' 'Will the protagonist be murdered by the fugitive?' The answer is generally provided in the climax; the dramatic question frames reader/viewer interest and stakes.

rubrics_metrics.name: First act — exposition and setup
rubrics_metrics.description: The first act is usually used for exposition, to establish the main characters, their relationships, and the world they live in.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Introduce protagonists, supporting cast, and context. Build enough grounding so the audience understands stakes and baseline before the inciting incident.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inciting incident (catalyst)
rubrics_metrics.description: A dynamic, on-screen incident occurs, known as the inciting incident, or catalyst, that confronts the main character (the protagonist).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The inciting incident confronts the protagonist and sets the story in motion; it should be a clear event that disturbs the status quo and propels the protagonist toward action.

rubrics_metrics.name: First plot point
rubrics_metrics.description: A first plot point signals the end of the first act, ensures that life will never be the same again for the protagonist, and raises a dramatic question that will be answered in the climax.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This turning point changes the protagonist's circumstances and frames the central problem or call to action (e.g., 'Will X recover the diamond?'). It marks commitment to the main story problem rather than returning to the status quo.

rubrics_metrics.name: Second act — rising action
rubrics_metrics.description: The second act, also referred to as 'rising action', typically depicts the protagonist's attempt to resolve the problem initiated by the first turning point, only to find themselves in ever worsening situations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use escalating obstacles and complications to maintain tension. The protagonist's attempts should fail or create new problems, increasing stakes and driving development toward the climax.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character development / character arc
rubrics_metrics.description: Protagonists must learn new skills and arrive at a higher sense of awareness of who they are and what they are capable of in order to deal with their predicament, which in turn changes who they are.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Character growth is achieved over the second act through challenges; refer to this as a character arc. Include catalysts for change and show measurable internal shifts, often aided by mentors or co-protagonists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Antagonism (forces opposing the protagonist)
rubrics_metrics.description: Part of the reason protagonists seem unable to resolve their problems is because they do not yet have the skills to deal with the forces of antagonism that confront them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Define clear antagonistic forces (people, circumstances, inner flaws). Use antagonism to create believable obstacles that force the protagonist to change or adapt.

rubrics_metrics.name: Third act — resolution and subplot closure
rubrics_metrics.description: The third act features the resolution of the story and its subplots.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Resolve the main plot and any significant subplots, delivering outcomes that follow from the climax and the protagonist's development. Avoid unresolved major threads unless intentionally left ambiguous.

rubrics_metrics.name: Climax
rubrics_metrics.description: The climax is the scene or sequence in which the main tensions of the story are brought to their most intense point and the dramatic question is answered, leaving the protagonist and other characters with a new sense of who they really are.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Position the climax toward the end of the third act; it should be the most intense confrontation or choice and should provide a clear answer to the dramatic question while reflecting the protagonist's arc.
